title: Production integration: how business systems call an agent on AgentCore
html:
Who this page is for: architects and developers who will connect an agent built in this workshop to their own business systems. This page is reference material, not a hands-on lab: options B, C and D below need permission to configure IAM or an identity provider (IdP), and participants have no AWS access at all in the workshop environment.

The Public API section of the Release chapter shows a business system calling the agent through Launchpad's /v1 API with an API key. That path fits demos and PoCs. Launchpad is sample code, not designed for production use, so production systems should not call agents through it. This page compares four ways to call an agent and gives a production recommendation.

Bottom line: in production use option B: the business system's own backend calls the AgentCore Runtime live endpoint directly with an IAM role (SigV4). When the end user's identity has to reach the agent and its downstream tools, use option D (the backend forwards the user's JWT). Option A is for demos and PoCs only; option C (browser calls directly) is not recommended for production.

1. Four ways to call an agent

Option In one sentence
A Through Launchpad /v1 The business backend calls Launchpad with a Launchpad API key, and Launchpad calls AgentCore (the path the Release chapter demonstrates)
B Business backend + IAM (recommended) The business backend signs with its own IAM role and calls AgentCore Runtime directly
C Browser + JWT, direct The front end calls AgentCore Runtime directly with the token the user got at sign-in
D Business backend + forwarded JWT The business backend verifies the user, then forwards the user's JWT to AgentCore Runtime 
flowchart LR
  U[A · Browser] --> BA[Business backend] -->|"X-Api-Key"| LP[Launchpad backend] -->|"SigV4 / JWT"| RT[(AgentCore Runtime)]
  U2[B · Browser] --> BB[Business backend] -->|"SigV4 (IAM role)"| RT2[(AgentCore Runtime)]
  U3[C · Browser] -->|"Bearer (user JWT)"| RT3[(AgentCore Runtime)]
  U4[D · Browser] --> BD[Business backend] -->|"Bearer (user JWT)"| RT4[(AgentCore Runtime)]

2. Call path

Aspect A B C D
Network hops 3, one extra through Launchpad 2 1 2
Latency Highest Low Lowest Low
Streaming Launchpad reads the Runtime stream, then re-sends it as SSE The business backend relays the Runtime's streamed response as is The front end reads it directly Same as B
Depends on Launchpad being up Yes: calls fail while Launchpad is unavailable No No No
Sessions Launchpad creates and returns session_id The business backend creates and stores runtimeSessionId The front end manages them The business backend manages them

3. Security

Aspect A B C D
Credential Long-lived static API key Temporary IAM role credentials, rotated automatically The user's short-lived JWT The user's short-lived JWT
Where it lives Business backend (never the browser) Business backend Browser, exposed to XSS Business backend
Scope The key belongs to the project the console was in when it was minted (it stops working once its creator is offboarded or the project is archived); the backend API can restrict it to agents, an expiry and a rate (agent_ids, expires_at, rate_per_minute), while the console can only create, enable and disable keys The IAM policy names one Runtime and endpoint ARN JWT audience / client allowlist Same as C, plus the business backend's own checks
Per-end-user authorization No: all users share one key The business backend's job; pass the user ID to the Runtime as runtimeUserId Yes Yes
Can Cedar policies on the Gateway decide per user No. There is no signed-in user behind /v1, so the Gateway sees one client identity; only console Chat exchanges a user token for the signed-in user No, same reason as A (see section 5) Yes Yes
Attack surface Launchpad's console and backend are on the call path Smallest The Runtime endpoint faces every end user directly; rate limiting and abuse protection rely on AgentCore alone Small
Audit Mostly the Launchpad ledger CloudTrail down to the role, business backend logs down to the user Only the user info inside the JWT; no central audit point on the business side CloudTrail plus business backend logs
Unexpected credential loss When the account that minted the key is deleted, disabled, expired or loses its workspace grant, the key is disabled automatically and production calls stop at once None Token expiry; the front end must refresh Refreshed centrally by the business backend

4. Architecture and operations

Aspect A B C D
Components on the production path Includes Launchpad: sample code, one EC2 instance under systemd Only AWS managed services and the business system's own backend Only AWS managed services Same as B
Availability Depends on the Launchpad host Depends on AgentCore and the business backend Depends on AgentCore Same as B
Scaling Launchpad can become the bottleneck Scale the business backend out Nothing to scale Same as B
Front-end work Small Small Large: token refresh, sessions and stream parsing all move to the front end; verify first that a browser can call this endpoint cross-origin Small
Back-end work One relay endpoint One relay endpoint plus an IAM role None One relay endpoint plus JWT validation
Runtime inbound auth No change No change: Runtimes that Launchpad deploys use IAM by default Switch to JWT Switch to JWT
Release control /v1 only calls the live endpoint Pass qualifier="live"; signing and rolling back at the release gate keep working Same as B Same as B
Data boundary Requests and answers pass through Launchpad Only the business system and AWS Same as B Same as B

A Runtime's inbound auth is one or the other: IAM (SigV4) or JWT. Once it is JWT, SigV4 calls are refused. Also, if the JWT issuer is not the Launchpad workspace's own Cognito user pool, every call that goes through Launchpad is refused (agent.inbound_issuer_mismatch), including console Chat, /v1 and evaluation.

5. What you must add yourself when you bypass Launchpad

Launchpad's call path does more than relay the request. Options B, C and D bypass it, so the business system has to take these over:

What Launchpad does on each call Without Launchpad
Builds the request body the way Launchpad-generated agents expect: {"prompt": ..., "actor_id": ...} The business backend sends the same shape. For a bring-your-own-code (BYOC) agent, use the fields its entrypoint actually reads
Uses <agent_id>__<username> as the Memory actor_id, so memories stay separate per agent and per user Pass actor_id by the same rule (for example <agent_id>__<business user ID>), or different users' memories mix
Sends runtimeUserId when the agent has Gateway tools or tools with outbound auth You must send it. Without it the Runtime injects no workload token, and the agent answers as usual without its Gateway tools, with no error
In console Chat, for an agent with Gateway tools, exchanges a Cognito user token for the signed-in user and puts it in the body as gateway_access_token, so Cedar can decide on the username or groups Under option B the Gateway sees one client identity, and per-user policies do not apply; use option D when you need them
Calls agents created as a managed Harness (method B) through the InvokeHarness API A different API: invoke_harness with harnessArn, runtimeSessionId, actorId and messages; the IAM action is bedrock-agentcore:InvokeHarness
For agents with PII protection on, screens the whole answer and masks it before returning it No screening. This protection is implemented in the Launchpad backend; add a guardrail in the business backend if you need it
When a curated-answer rule matches, returns the curated answer without calling the model Does not apply; every call goes to the model
Records sessions in its ledger, behind console Chat history and the API keys' last-used time No such records. The Runtime's logs and traces in CloudWatch are still there (log group /aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/<runtime-id>-<endpoint name>)

6. Production recommendation: option B

  1. No sample code on the production path. Launchpad stays in the development workflow, where agents are created, evaluated and released; business traffic calls AgentCore directly.
  2. The safest credential. Temporary IAM credentials, no long-lived secret; permissions scoped to one Runtime and endpoint; every call audited in CloudTrail.
  3. No change to the agent. Runtimes that Launchpad deploys use IAM auth by default.
  4. The release gate keeps working. The business backend always calls the live endpoint. When release-ops signs or rolls back on the release gate page, that changes the version live points to, with no change on the business side.
  5. Central control. Rate limiting, content moderation and logging live in one place, the business backend.

6.1 IAM policy (the business backend's role)

json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "InvokeOneAgent",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime",
        "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:<account-id>:runtime/<runtime-id>",
        "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:<account-id>:runtime/<runtime-id>/runtime-endpoint/live"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser is needed only when calls pass runtimeUserId. The Runtime ID and ARN are on the agent's detail page in the console.

6.2 Business backend example (Python / FastAPI, streamed relay)

python
import json
import uuid

import boto3
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

AGENT_ID = "<launchpad-agent-id>"   # prefix of the Memory actor_id
RUNTIME_ARN = "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:<account-id>:runtime/<runtime-id>"
client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-east-1")
app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/api/assistant/chat")
def chat(body: dict, user=Depends(current_user)):  # current_user: the business system's own sign-in check
    # keep one id per conversation (33+ characters); stored by the backend, not taken blindly from the client
    session_id = body.get("session_id") or str(uuid.uuid4())
    resp = client.invoke_agent_runtime(
        agentRuntimeArn=RUNTIME_ARN,
        qualifier="live",                 # follows the release gate: signing and rollback move this endpoint
        runtimeSessionId=session_id,
        runtimeUserId=user.id,            # required when the agent has Gateway tools
        payload=json.dumps({
            "prompt": body["prompt"],
            "actor_id": f"{AGENT_ID}__{user.id}",  # Memory separated per agent and per user
        }).encode(),
    )
    stream = resp["response"]
    return StreamingResponse(
        stream.iter_chunks(),             # relay the Runtime's streamed response as is
        media_type=resp.get("contentType", "application/json"),
        headers={"X-Session-Id": session_id},
    )

This only shows the call. Before going live, add session ownership checks (so a user cannot continue someone else's session_id), timeouts (one answer can take minutes), error handling and rate limiting.

7. When to use option D instead

Use option D when either is true:

  • Cedar policies on the Gateway must allow or deny by the end user's username or groups (for example "only the finance group may call the payout tool");
  • Downstream tools must reach third-party systems as the end user (OBO token exchange).

How: on the agent's page in Launchpad, switch inbound auth to JWT and enter the enterprise IdP's discovery URL and the allowed audience or client (the ARN stays the same; a new version is created). After the business backend verifies the user's sign-in, it forwards the user's access token to the data-plane endpoint:

text
POST https://bedrock-agentcore.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/runtimes/<URL-encoded Runtime ARN>/invocations?qualifier=live
Authorization: Bearer <the user's access token>
X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Id: <session id>
Content-Type: application/json

{"prompt": "...", "actor_id": "<agent_id>__<user ID>"}

Mind the limit in the warning box in section 4: if the JWT issuer is not the workspace's own Cognito user pool, console Chat, /v1 and evaluation can no longer call this agent. The simplest way around it is to have the business system use the workspace's Cognito user pool too.

8. Go-live checklist

  • The business backend's role has only the permissions in section 6.1, scoped to this one Runtime and its live endpoint.
  • Every call passes qualifier="live"; versions change only through signing and rollback at the release gate.
  • The backend creates and stores runtimeSessionId, and checks that the session belongs to the current user.
  • actor_id is passed as <agent_id>__<user ID>; when the agent has Gateway tools, runtimeUserId is passed too.
  • Check whether the agent relies on Launchpad-side PII protection or curated answers; if it does, add the equivalent in the business backend.
  • The business backend has rate limiting, request size limits and timeouts, with WAF or API Gateway in front of the public entry point.
  • AgentCore Observability is on, and business logs record session_id so they can be matched to traces in CloudWatch.
  • Where private networking is required, the business backend reaches AgentCore through a VPC endpoint (PrivateLink).
